segments.line: Then
you make a mistake. You start selling
at the chariot races. The Circus Maximus seats around a hundred and fifty thousand people. That's real.
Felix and his friends run up and down the stands with baskets of burgers, shouting your name.
By the fourth race, the crowd isn't cheering for the chariots anymore.
They're chanting. Burgus! Burgus! Burgus!
And up in the emperor's box, someone notices.
The next morning, a man in a white toga with a wide purple stripe is sitting at your counter. He doesn't order. He's from the palace.
He explains how Rome works.
The emperor keeps the people quiet with two things: free food, and shows.
A Roman poet called it bread and circuses. That's real.
Every month, the state hands out free grain to about two hundred thousand men in this city. That's real too.
'The people love your food, ' he says. 'So from tomorrow, it's the emperor's food. '
He slides a wax tablet across the counter. A contract.
Burgus Maximus becomes property of the palace. You'll cook for the emperor,
live in a house on the Palatine Hill, and never worry about money again.
Every other cookshop on the street will be closed, by order.
Tullia looks at you. She doesn't say a word. She knows those cooks. She's known them all her life.
You say you need to think about it. 'Of course, ' he says.
Then he smiles at Ellie, and gives her a honey cake.
'What a sweet girl. Rome can be so dangerous for children. '
